analysis.one_liner: Federal-state grants to cover college costs so in-state public students graduate without debt.
analysis.headline: The Debt-Free College Act of 2023 never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the Senate HELP Committee on the day it was introduced and died there when Congress ended January 3, 2025 [S1] [S5].
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created federal grants matching each state's spending on public higher education, with states committing to cover whatever federal, state, and local grant aid doesn't cover — so students at in-state public colleges graduate without loans. It also would have sent grants to historically Black colleges and minority-serving institutions to cover their students' unmet costs, capped public college tuition with only inflation-based increases, and made students who came to the U.S. as children (Dreamers) eligible for federal financial aid. It authorized $84 billion in year one plus $3 billion for HBCUs and minority-serving institutions, and sums as necessary through 2033.
analysis.who_benefits: Students at in-state public colleges — especially Pell Grant recipients and low-income students, whose unmet need would be covered first — plus students at historically Black colleges and minority-serving institutions, and Dreamer students who would gain federal aid eligibility for the first time.
analysis.who_benefits_short: In-state public college students, especially low-income ones

how_it_helps.text: States that join the partnership get a federal grant equal to their own annual operating support for public higher education, and must cover the unmet need — the gap between what college costs and what a student's family and existing grant aid provides — for every eligible in-state public college student [S2] [S3].

Pell Grant recipients get covered first, and states must maintain access for low-income and underserved students; leftover funds go to non-Pell students by financial need, ignoring private scholarships when calculating need [S3].
Participating states must cap tuition and fees at in-state public colleges at 2023 levels, allowing only CPI-based increases, and work to reduce tuition as state support grows [S3].

Historically Black colleges and universities and minority-serving institutions could receive grants covering their students' unmet need, with 95% of funds going to need-based aid for students without a bachelor's degree [S2] [S3].

Dreamer students — those who entered the U.S. before age 16, met school and education criteria, or served four years in uniformed services — would become eligible for federal student aid, which current law bars them from [S2] [S3].
4% of state grant funds must go to student success programs — advisors, tutors, child care, transportation, emergency grants — aimed at raising completion rates for low-income students [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through $84 billion in year one and additional sums through 2033; state taxpayers must also maintain their current levels of higher-education funding to keep receiving grants, and states would face tuition caps limiting their public universities' ability to raise tuition revenue.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; states must keep funding levels

drawbacks.text: The cost is enormous: $84 billion for fiscal 2024 alone plus 'such sums as may be necessary' through 2033, and the federal grant formula matches a state's entire operating support dollar-for-dollar, so wealthier states with heavy spending would receive the largest grants [S3].

Matching grants proportional to existing state spending reward states that already invest the most, so high-spending states would draw down the most federal money, and the bill's authorized sums were never funded by any appropriations process [S2] [S3].

Extending federal student aid to Dreamer students was certain to draw strong political opposition, and states would have to maintain existing need-based aid programs and keep tuition capped, which in some states would require shifting funds from other priorities [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — eliminating the need for student loans at in-state public colleges for all comers, weighted toward the poorest students — is large and concrete, and the bill includes real guardrails: states must maintain their own funding, tuition is capped, and there are probation and ineligibility provisions for states that break the partnership. The drawback is that it is one of the most expensive versions of debt-free college proposed, with no new revenue identified, and the matching formula sends more federal dollars to states that already spend the most on higher ed. Whether that trade is worth it is a legitimate policy argument; what is not arguable is that it never got a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or a vote, and expired when the 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025 [S5] [S1].

narrative.text: Sen. Brian Schatz introduced the bill June 7, 2023, with six Democratic cosponsors, all Democrats [S1] [S4].
The Senate's only action was to read it twice and refer it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever followed [S5].
The 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025, and the bill died in committee [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained a program, but the status quo held: the federal government kept roughly $84 billion a year it would otherwise have spent on college grants, loan servicers and lenders kept a student loan system untouched, and states kept full control of tuition levels. Students who would have gotten debt-free aid got nothing from this bill's death, but nothing was taken from anyone either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers kept the money; lenders kept their market

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced past committee referral [S4] [S5].

industries.note: A debt-free guarantee at in-state public colleges would shrink the population of students who need to borrow, reducing loan origination and servicing volume. The bill died before touching this market.

State grants equal to operating support plus tuition caps backed by federal money would fund institutions while limiting their tuition revenue growth; 4% of grant funds would flow to student success programs on campus.
A separate $3 billion grant stream would cover unmet need at eligible institutions, with tuition caps and maintenance-of-effort requirements attached.
Institutions that converted from for-profit to nonprofit status within 25 years are excluded from the HBCU/MSI grant program, and state grant funds may not support students at proprietary schools.
